questions.stem:
A microbiology lab tests a panel of drugs against two reference organisms grown under the conditions each prefers. Organism 1 is an obligate aerobe, and organism 2 is an obligate anaerobe. Drug P kills organism 2 but has no effect on organism 1, even at high concentrations and even though organism 1 has never been exposed to it. Neither organism carries plasmids or resistance genes.

Which drug is P most likely, and why does organism 1 resist it?
choices: Metronidazole, because the aerobe cannot reduce the drug to its active form
Gentamicin, because the aerobe lacks the oxidative metabolism to take it up
Vancomycin, because the aerobe's outer membrane keeps the drug from its target
Aztreonam, because the aerobe's penicillin-binding proteins do not bind it
Ceftriaxone, because the aerobe produces a chromosomal carbapenemase
questions.note:
**Intrinsic resistance is a species trait: aerobes resist metronidazole (cannot reduce it), anaerobes resist aminoglycosides (no uptake), Gram-negatives resist vancomycin, and Gram-positives resist aztreonam.**

With no acquired genes, this is intrinsic resistance: a normal structural or functional trait of the species. The lecture's examples include metronidazole, a prodrug that must be reduced anaerobically to become active, so aerobic bacteria are intrinsically resistant to it. Organism 2, an anaerobe, activates and is killed by it.

The other examples run the opposite way or concern other barriers: anaerobes resist aminoglycosides because they lack the oxidative metabolism to take them up, vancomycin cannot cross the Gram-negative outer membrane, and aztreonam does not bind Gram-positive PBPs. None of those fits a drug that kills the anaerobe and spares the aerobe.

Metronidazole, because the aerobe cannot reduce the drug to its active form: correct. Metronidazole needs anaerobic reduction to its active form, so aerobes are intrinsically resistant.

Gentamicin, because the aerobe lacks the oxidative metabolism to take it up: incorrect. Aminoglycoside uptake needs oxidative metabolism, so they kill aerobes and spare anaerobes, the reverse of this result.

Vancomycin, because the aerobe's outer membrane keeps the drug from its target: incorrect. The vancomycin barrier is the Gram-negative outer membrane, which has nothing to do with oxygen use.

Aztreonam, because the aerobe's penicillin-binding proteins do not bind it: incorrect. Aztreonam's barrier is Gram-positive PBPs, not aerobic metabolism.

Ceftriaxone, because the aerobe produces a chromosomal carbapenemase: incorrect. A carbapenemase is an acquired enzyme, and the stem rules out resistance genes.

questions.stem:
A 72-year-old woman in a long-term care facility with an indwelling urinary catheter develops urosepsis. Urine and blood grow a lactose-fermenting, encapsulated Gram-negative rod that is resistant to imipenem, meropenem and ertapenem. Molecular testing shows two changes: a gene for an enzyme that hydrolyzes all beta-lactams, and reduced production of outer membrane channel proteins.

How does the second change contribute to resistance?
choices: It alters the penicillin-binding proteins so the drug no longer binds
It adds acetyl groups to the drug so that it no longer binds its target
It actively pumps the drug from the cytoplasm back out of the cell
It slows passive entry of the drug across the outer membrane
It replaces terminal D-alanine with D-lactate in the cell wall precursors
questions.note:
**Enterobacteriaceae become carbapenem resistant by producing carbapenemases (such as KPC) and by reducing or altering outer membrane porins that carbapenems pass through.**

A carbapenem-resistant, encapsulated, lactose-fermenting Gram-negative rod in a catheterized nursing home resident is a carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae (CRE), most likely *Klebsiella pneumoniae*. The lecture names two mechanisms of carbapenem resistance in Enterobacteriaceae: production of a carbapenemase (such as KPC, *Klebsiella pneumoniae* carbapenemase, which hydrolyzes all beta-lactams) and alteration or reduction of porins.

Porins are beta-barrel channels in the Gram-negative outer membrane through which beta-lactams passively diffuse to reach their PBPs. Fewer or narrower porins mean less drug reaches the periplasm, and together with an enzyme that destroys the drug that does get in, resistance is high.

It alters the penicillin-binding proteins so the drug no longer binds: incorrect. Altered PBPs are a resistance mechanism, but the stem describes fewer outer membrane channels.

It adds acetyl groups to the drug so that it no longer binds its target: incorrect. Acetylating enzymes are aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes, not porin changes.

It actively pumps the drug from the cytoplasm back out of the cell: incorrect. Efflux pumps actively expel drug; porins are passive entry channels.

It slows passive entry of the drug across the outer membrane: correct. Reduced porins limit passive diffusion of carbapenems to their PBP targets.

It replaces terminal D-alanine with D-lactate in the cell wall precursors: incorrect. D-Ala-D-Lac substitution is the vancomycin resistance mechanism in VRE.

questions.stem:
A hospital lab tests a urinary Klebsiella isolate.

Ampicillin: Resistant
Ceftriaxone: Resistant
Cefepime: Resistant
Aztreonam: Resistant
Meropenem: Susceptible
Ceftriaxone plus clavulanic acid (test well): Activity restored

Which enzyme best explains this pattern?
choices: A penicillinase that hydrolyzes only penicillins
A metallo-beta-lactamase that requires zinc
An extended-spectrum beta-lactamase
A carbapenemase such as KPC
An altered penicillin-binding protein 2a
questions.note:
**ESBLs confer resistance to penicillins, cephalosporins and aztreonam, are inhibited by clavulanate, tazobactam or sulbactam, and leave carbapenems active.**

The lecture describes extended-spectrum beta-lactamases (ESBLs) as enzymes that confer resistance to penicillins, cephalosporins and the monobactam aztreonam, can be inhibited by clavulanic acid, tazobactam or sulbactam, and spare the carbapenems. This isolate matches every feature: resistant to ampicillin, third- and fourth-generation cephalosporins and aztreonam, susceptible to meropenem, with activity restored by clavulanate.

A carbapenemase or metallo-beta-lactamase would also destroy meropenem, a simple penicillinase would leave cephalosporins active, and PBP2a is a *Staphylococcus aureus* target change, not a Gram-negative enzyme.

A penicillinase that hydrolyzes only penicillins: incorrect. A penicillinase would leave ceftriaxone, cefepime and aztreonam active.

A metallo-beta-lactamase that requires zinc: incorrect. Metallo-beta-lactamases are carbapenemases and would make meropenem fail.

An extended-spectrum beta-lactamase: correct. ESBLs hydrolyze penicillins, cephalosporins and aztreonam, spare carbapenems and are inhibited by clavulanate.

A carbapenemase such as KPC: incorrect. A carbapenemase such as KPC would hydrolyze meropenem too.

An altered penicillin-binding protein 2a: incorrect. PBP2a is the MRSA target alteration, not a Gram-negative enzyme.

questions.stem:
A 64-year-old man on a ventilator develops pneumonia. Sputum grows Klebsiella pneumoniae that is resistant to all carbapenems and is documented to produce a Klebsiella pneumoniae carbapenemase. Susceptibility testing shows the isolate remains susceptible to a newer combination of a beta-lactam with a beta-lactamase inhibitor.

Which agent is that combination?
choices: Amoxicillin-clavulanate
Ampicillin-sulbactam
Piperacillin-tazobactam
Imipenem-cilastatin
Ceftazidime-avibactam
questions.note:
**CRE treatment is limited to tigecycline, fosfomycin, aminoglycosides and newer combinations such as ceftazidime-avibactam and meropenem-vaborbactam.**

Carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae that produce a carbapenemase leave very few options. The lecture lists tigecycline, fosfomycin and aminoglycosides, plus newer beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitor combinations: ceftazidime-avibactam and meropenem-vaborbactam, both with activity against KPC producers.

Older inhibitors (clavulanate, sulbactam, tazobactam) do not protect against carbapenemases, and cilastatin is not a beta-lactamase inhibitor at all; it blocks renal dehydropeptidase.

Amoxicillin-clavulanate: incorrect. Clavulanate does not inhibit carbapenemases such as KPC.

Ampicillin-sulbactam: incorrect. Sulbactam does not protect ampicillin from a KPC enzyme.

Piperacillin-tazobactam: incorrect. Tazobactam does not overcome KPC carbapenemases.

Imipenem-cilastatin: incorrect. Cilastatin blocks renal dehydropeptidase, and imipenem is hydrolyzed by the carbapenemase.

Ceftazidime-avibactam: correct. Ceftazidime-avibactam is a newer combination with activity against KPC-producing CRE.

questions.stem:
A 22-year-old college wrestler has a tender, fluctuant, draining abscess on his thigh. Two teammates had similar lesions. After incision and drainage, culture grows Gram-positive cocci in clusters that are coagulase positive and resistant to oxacillin. He is well appearing and afebrile and will be treated at home.

Which oral antibiotic is an appropriate choice?
choices: Dicloxacillin
Cephalexin
Amoxicillin-clavulanate
Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole
Vancomycin capsules taken by mouth
questions.note:
**Vancomycin is first choice for serious MRSA infection; oral home options include TMP-SMX, clindamycin, doxycycline and minocycline; all standard beta-lactams fail.**

A draining abscess in a contact-sport athlete with affected teammates, growing oxacillin-resistant *S. aureus*, is community-acquired MRSA. Crowded living, athletics and close contact are risk factors the lecture lists. Intravenous vancomycin is the first-choice drug for serious MRSA infection, but for home use the lecture lists the oral options trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, clindamycin, minocycline and doxycycline.

All beta-lactams, including dicloxacillin, cephalexin and inhibitor combinations, fail against MRSA because of PBP2a. Oral vancomycin is not absorbed and treats only *C. difficile*.

Dicloxacillin: incorrect. Dicloxacillin is an anti-staphylococcal penicillin; MRSA resists it through PBP2a.

Cephalexin: incorrect. Cephalexin is a first-generation cephalosporin and does not cover MRSA.

Amoxicillin-clavulanate: incorrect. Clavulanate blocks beta-lactamases but does not overcome PBP2a.

Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole: correct. TMP-SMX is one of the oral drugs used at home for MRSA skin infections.

Vancomycin capsules taken by mouth: incorrect. Oral vancomycin is not absorbed and is used only for *C. difficile*.

questions.stem:
A 59-year-old woman with a long hospital stay develops a urinary catheter-associated bacteremia. Blood cultures grow Enterococcus faecium that is resistant to vancomycin and to ampicillin. She has no lung involvement.

Which drug is an appropriate treatment option for this infection?
choices: Ceftriaxone
Daptomycin
Aztreonam
Cefazolin
Clindamycin
questions.note:
**VRE is treated with ampicillin if susceptible, otherwise daptomycin, linezolid, tigecycline or eravacycline.**

For vancomycin-resistant *Enterococcus* (VRE), the lecture's approach is ampicillin first if the isolate is still ampicillin susceptible, and otherwise daptomycin, linezolid, tigecycline or eravacycline. This isolate is ampicillin resistant, so daptomycin (a good choice for bacteremia without pneumonia) fits.

Enterococci are intrinsically resistant to cephalosporins (no reliable enterococcal coverage) and to clindamycin, and aztreonam has no Gram-positive activity.

Ceftriaxone: incorrect. Cephalosporins have no reliable enterococcal activity.

Daptomycin: correct. Daptomycin is one of the listed options for VRE when ampicillin cannot be used.

Aztreonam: incorrect. Aztreonam has no Gram-positive activity.

Cefazolin: incorrect. Cefazolin, like all cephalosporins, does not reliably cover *Enterococcus*.

Clindamycin: incorrect. Enterococci are intrinsically resistant to clindamycin.

questions.stem:
Researchers sequence a multidrug-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii isolate that is resistant to ciprofloxacin and trimethoprim. They find point mutations in two chromosomal genes. Purified enzyme from each mutant gene still carries out its normal reaction at nearly normal rates, but each drug now binds its enzyme far less tightly.

Which two genes are most likely mutated?
choices: Penicillin-binding protein and porin genes
30S ribosomal protein and efflux pump genes
DNA gyrase and dihydrofolate reductase genes
Dihydropteroate synthase and RNA polymerase genes
Beta-lactamase and aminoglycoside-modifying enzyme genes
questions.note:
**Target site mutations that lower drug binding but preserve enzyme function cause fluoroquinolone resistance (DNA gyrase, topoisomerase IV) and trimethoprim resistance (dihydrofolate reductase).**

Ciprofloxacin targets DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV; trimethoprim targets dihydrofolate reductase. The lecture describes target site alteration in *A. baumannii*: point mutations in DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV cause fluoroquinolone resistance, and mutations in dihydrofolate reductase cause trimethoprim resistance.

The key principle is in the stem: these mutations sharply reduce drug binding while leaving the enzyme's normal activity mostly intact, so the bacterium keeps the function and loses the vulnerability.

Penicillin-binding protein and porin genes: incorrect. PBP and porin changes cause beta-lactam resistance, not fluoroquinolone or trimethoprim resistance.

30S ribosomal protein and efflux pump genes: incorrect. Efflux can contribute, but efflux pumps and 30S proteins are not the targets of these two drugs.

DNA gyrase and dihydrofolate reductase genes: correct. Gyrase mutations cause fluoroquinolone resistance and dihydrofolate reductase mutations cause trimethoprim resistance.

Dihydropteroate synthase and RNA polymerase genes: incorrect. Dihydropteroate synthase is the sulfonamide target, and RNA polymerase is not targeted by either drug.

Beta-lactamase and aminoglycoside-modifying enzyme genes: incorrect. Beta-lactamases and AMEs are drug-destroying or drug-modifying enzymes, not altered targets.

questions.stem:
A hospital lab reports an Acinetobacter baumannii isolate tested against seven standard antimicrobial categories for this organism. It is non-susceptible to at least one agent in each of these categories: aminoglycosides, antipseudomonal penicillins with inhibitors, cephalosporins, carbapenems, fluoroquinolones and folate inhibitors. It remains susceptible to the agents in one category, the glycylcyclines (tigecycline).

How should this isolate be classified?
choices: Susceptible, because one category still works
Multidrug resistant but not extensively drug resistant
Intrinsically resistant
Pan-drug resistant
Extensively drug resistant
questions.note:
**MDR is non-susceptibility in 3 or more categories, XDR leaves only 1 or 2 categories active, and PDR is non-susceptibility to all categories.**

The lecture defines three tiers. Multidrug resistant (MDR) is acquired non-susceptibility to at least one agent in three or more categories. Extensively drug resistant (XDR) is non-susceptibility to at least one agent in all but two or fewer categories, meaning only one or two categories still work. Pan-drug resistant (PDR) is non-susceptibility to every agent in every category.

This isolate is non-susceptible in six of seven categories and susceptible only to tigecycline, so it is XDR. It also technically meets the MDR threshold, but XDR is the more specific label. That matches the lecture's note that tigecycline is often a last option against carbapenem-resistant *Acinetobacter*.

Susceptible, because one category still works: incorrect. Non-susceptibility in six categories is far beyond a susceptible isolate.

Multidrug resistant but not extensively drug resistant: incorrect. It exceeds the MDR threshold; with only one category left, XDR is the correct label.

Intrinsically resistant: incorrect. This is acquired resistance across many classes, not a species trait.

Pan-drug resistant: incorrect. PDR requires non-susceptibility to all agents in all categories, and tigecycline still works.

Extensively drug resistant: correct. Susceptible in only one or two categories defines extensively drug resistant.

questions.stem:
A carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii isolate is also resistant to fluoroquinolones, tetracyclines, erythromycin and tigecycline. When researchers add an experimental compound that blocks a tripartite membrane transporter spanning the inner membrane, periplasm and outer membrane, the minimum inhibitory concentrations of all of these unrelated drugs fall together.

Which resistance mechanism does this experiment reveal?
choices: A single enzyme that hydrolyzes all of these drug classes at once
Overexpressed multidrug efflux pumps that expel the drugs
Low-affinity penicillin-binding proteins that ignore the drugs
Loss of porins that these drugs need to cross the outer membrane
Point mutations in one shared ribosomal target of these drugs
questions.note:
**MDR Acinetobacter overexpresses multidrug efflux pumps that expel aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, tetracyclines, erythromycin, trimethoprim and tigecycline.**

When resistance to many unrelated classes collapses at once after blocking a transporter that spans both membranes, the mechanism is efflux. The lecture notes that overproduction of multidrug efflux pumps is common in *A. baumannii*; they remove drug from the cytoplasm or periplasm and reduce its effective concentration. The drugs listed as effluxed include aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, tetracyclines, chloramphenicol, erythromycin, trimethoprim and tigecycline.

Because one pump handles many structurally different drugs, efflux pump inhibitors are an attractive future strategy, which is the point the lecture makes about future drugs.

A single enzyme that hydrolyzes all of these drug classes at once: incorrect. No single enzyme destroys fluoroquinolones, tetracyclines and macrolides; beta-lactamases act on beta-lactams.

Overexpressed multidrug efflux pumps that expel the drugs: correct. Overexpressed multidrug efflux pumps expel many unrelated drugs, and blocking them restores activity.

Low-affinity penicillin-binding proteins that ignore the drugs: incorrect. Low-affinity PBPs affect beta-lactams only, and none of these drugs binds PBPs.

Loss of porins that these drugs need to cross the outer membrane: incorrect. Porin loss limits entry but would not be reversed by blocking an export transporter.

Point mutations in one shared ribosomal target of these drugs: incorrect. These drugs have different targets (gyrase, 30S, 50S), so one shared target mutation is impossible.

questions.stem:
Two Staphylococcus aureus isolates are compared. Isolate 1 is resistant to penicillin but susceptible to oxacillin, cefazolin and amoxicillin-clavulanate. Isolate 2 is resistant to penicillin, oxacillin, cefazolin, amoxicillin-clavulanate and meropenem. Both carry a plasmid-borne transposon encoding the same enzyme, but only isolate 2 carries a second, chromosomal gene.

What does the second gene in isolate 2 encode, and why does it defeat even inhibitor combinations?
choices: A penicillin-binding protein whose active site is shielded from typical beta-lactams
A carbapenemase that hydrolyzes every beta-lactam, even inhibitor-protected ones
An efflux pump that removes beta-lactams from the periplasm before they act
A ligase that makes D-alanyl-D-lactate precursors the drugs cannot bind
A porin mutation that keeps beta-lactams from crossing the outer membrane
questions.note:
**S. aureus resists beta-lactams by the plasmid-borne PC1 penicillinase (blocked by inhibitors) and by mecA-encoded PBP2a, an altered target that makes MRSA resistant to all beta-lactams.**

The lecture gives *S. aureus* two beta-lactam resistance mechanisms. The first is PC1, a penicillinase carried on a transposon on a plasmid, nearly universal in staphylococci and susceptible to beta-lactamase inhibitors. That explains isolate 1: penicillin fails, but oxacillin, cefazolin and amoxicillin-clavulanate still work (MSSA).

The second is acquisition of the *mecA* gene encoding PBP2a, an altered PBP with an extra loop that blocks the transpeptidase active site from molecules the size of typical beta-lactams while keeping normal enzyme function. That makes isolate 2 MRSA, resistant to all beta-lactams, and because the problem is the target and not an enzyme, adding a beta-lactamase inhibitor does not help.

A penicillin-binding protein whose active site is shielded from typical beta-lactams: correct. *mecA* encodes PBP2a, whose shielded active site ignores typical beta-lactams, so inhibitors cannot help.

A carbapenemase that hydrolyzes every beta-lactam, even inhibitor-protected ones: incorrect. Carbapenemases are a Gram-negative (CRE) mechanism, not how MRSA resists.

An efflux pump that removes beta-lactams from the periplasm before they act: incorrect. Efflux is a Gram-negative strategy in this lecture, and staphylococci have no periplasm or outer membrane.

A ligase that makes D-alanyl-D-lactate precursors the drugs cannot bind: incorrect. D-Ala-D-Lac precursors cause vancomycin resistance, not beta-lactam resistance.

A porin mutation that keeps beta-lactams from crossing the outer membrane: incorrect. *S. aureus* is Gram-positive and has no outer membrane porins.

questions.stem:
A 68-year-old man in the intensive care unit for 3 weeks, who has received long courses of vancomycin and cephalosporins, develops bacteremia. Blood cultures grow Gram-positive cocci in pairs and short chains that are catalase negative, gamma-hemolytic and grow in 6.5% sodium chloride. The isolate is E. faecium. Vancomycin MIC is far above the susceptible range.

Which change in this organism best explains its resistance to the drug he was receiving?
choices: Production of a beta-lactamase that hydrolyzes the drug
Mutation of PBP2a so that the drug cannot reach the active site
Peptidoglycan precursors ending in D-alanyl-D-lactate
Aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes that acetylate the drug
Loss of outer membrane porins that the drug uses for entry
questions.note:
**VRE (mostly E. faecium) replace D-Ala-D-Ala with D-Ala-D-Lac in peptidoglycan precursors, lowering vancomycin binding about 1,000-fold.**

Catalase-negative, gamma-hemolytic cocci in pairs and chains that tolerate 6.5% NaCl are enterococci, and *E. faecium* is the species that accounts for most vancomycin-resistant *Enterococcus* (VRE). Prior vancomycin, cephalosporins, long ICU stays and invasive devices are listed risk factors.

Vancomycin binds the D-Ala-D-Ala terminus of peptidoglycan precursors. VRE carry a gene cluster that builds D-Ala-D-Lac instead and incorporates it into the wall, which lowers vancomycin binding about 1,000-fold while cell wall synthesis continues normally.

Production of a beta-lactamase that hydrolyzes the drug: incorrect. Vancomycin is not a beta-lactam, so beta-lactamases do not affect it.

Mutation of PBP2a so that the drug cannot reach the active site: incorrect. PBP2a is the MRSA beta-lactam mechanism; vancomycin does not bind PBPs.

Peptidoglycan precursors ending in D-alanyl-D-lactate: correct. D-Ala-D-Lac precursors lower vancomycin binding about 1,000-fold.

Aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes that acetylate the drug: incorrect. Aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes act on aminoglycosides, mainly in Gram-negatives.

Loss of outer membrane porins that the drug uses for entry: incorrect. Enterococci are Gram-positive and have no outer membrane porins.

questions.stem:
A 47-year-old man with extensive burns in the intensive care unit develops ventilator-associated pneumonia. Cultures grow a non-motile, aerobic, oxidase-negative Gram-negative coccobacillus that persisted on bed rails despite routine disinfectant cleaning. The isolate is resistant to gentamicin and tobramycin. Analysis of the drug recovered from the culture shows that the gentamicin molecules have acquired acetyl and phosphate groups.

Which statement about this resistance is correct?
choices: It is caused by mutation of the 30S subunit so the drug cannot bind
It is the main mode of aminoglycoside resistance in this organism
It is caused by D-alanyl-D-lactate precursors in the cell wall
It is intrinsic, because aerobes cannot take up aminoglycosides
It can be reversed by adding clavulanic acid to the aminoglycoside
questions.note:
**Aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes (acetyl-, phospho-, adenyltransferases) are the main mode of aminoglycoside resistance in MDR Acinetobacter baumannii.**

An oxidase-negative Gram-negative coccobacillus that causes ventilator-associated pneumonia in burn patients and survives disinfectants is *Acinetobacter baumannii*, an ESKAPE pathogen. The drug itself carries new acetyl and phosphate groups, which identifies aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes (AMEs), acetyltransferases, phosphotransferases and adenyltransferases often carried on transposable elements.

The lecture calls AMEs the main mode of aminoglycoside resistance in multidrug-resistant *A. baumannii*, with efflux pumps and rRNA-modifying enzymes as other mechanisms. A chemically altered drug can no longer bind its target properly.

It is caused by mutation of the 30S subunit so the drug cannot bind: incorrect. Ribosomal changes exist, but the stem shows the drug itself was chemically modified.

It is the main mode of aminoglycoside resistance in this organism: correct. Aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes are the main mode of aminoglycoside resistance in *A. baumannii*.

It is caused by D-alanyl-D-lactate precursors in the cell wall: incorrect. D-Ala-D-Lac is the vancomycin resistance mechanism.

It is intrinsic, because aerobes cannot take up aminoglycosides: incorrect. Intrinsic aminoglycoside resistance belongs to anaerobes, which lack oxidative uptake; this aerobe acquired enzymes.

It can be reversed by adding clavulanic acid to the aminoglycoside: incorrect. Clavulanate inhibits beta-lactamases and has no effect on aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes.

questions.stem:
A 70-year-old man with COPD and diabetes has been in the intensive care unit for 2 weeks with a central line and urinary catheter. He develops fever and hypotension. A prior culture grew a motile, oxidase-positive, non-lactose-fermenting Gram-negative rod that made a blue-green pigment and resisted several drug classes. Cultures are pending, and the team must start empiric therapy now.

Which empiric approach does the lecture recommend for this high-risk patient?
choices: Two drugs from different classes, each with activity against Pseudomonas
A single carbapenem, since it covers every Gram-negative rod
Vancomycin plus daptomycin to cover any resistant organism
Ceftriaxone plus metronidazole for Gram-negatives and anaerobes
Tigecycline alone, as the last-option agent for MDR rods
questions.note:
**High-risk patients with possible MDR Pseudomonas are treated empirically with two antipseudomonal drugs from different classes (for example, an aminoglycoside plus piperacillin-tazobactam).**

The described organism is *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*: motile, oxidase positive, non-lactose fermenting, blue-green pigment (pyocyanin). Risk factors for multidrug-resistant *Pseudomonas* include a prolonged ICU stay, invasive devices, underlying disease such as diabetes and COPD, and older age, and this patient has all of them.

The lecture recommends that high-risk patients be treated empirically with two different drug classes that both cover *Pseudomonas*, for example an aminoglycoside plus piperacillin-tazobactam, so that at least one will likely work while susceptibilities are pending. Resistance mechanisms parallel *Acinetobacter*: beta-lactamases, AMEs, efflux, porin loss and target changes.

Two drugs from different classes, each with activity against Pseudomonas: correct. High-risk patients get two antipseudomonal drugs from different classes, such as an aminoglycoside plus piperacillin-tazobactam.

A single carbapenem, since it covers every Gram-negative rod: incorrect. MDR *Pseudomonas* can be carbapenem resistant, so one agent alone risks failure.

Vancomycin plus daptomycin to cover any resistant organism: incorrect. Vancomycin and daptomycin have no Gram-negative activity.

Ceftriaxone plus metronidazole for Gram-negatives and anaerobes: incorrect. Ceftriaxone has no *Pseudomonas* activity.

Tigecycline alone, as the last-option agent for MDR rods: incorrect. Tigecycline does not cover *Pseudomonas* (one of the "4 Ps").
